newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU calls Anglo/Lonrho report speculation.
newsitem.headline: EU calls Anglo/Lonrho report speculation.

text.p: A European Commission spokesman said on Monday that a British press report that the Commission will block a 28-percent stake held by South African mining group Anglo American Corp in rival company Lonrho Plc was "pure speculation".

He said the Commission's merger task force, which prepares decisions for the Commission, had not reached any final conclusions. The deadline for the Commission to rule on Anglo's stake was May 5, he said.

The Commission said in December that Anglo's shareholding gave it control of Lonrho and its platinum division although the South African company denies this. The Commission at the time expressed fears the deal would create a dominant position in the market for the precious metal.

The Independent On Sunday quoted an unnamed source on Sunday as saying that European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert had stated privately that he would not allow Anglo to make use of its stake.

Anglo American increased its Lonrho shareholding to 28.4 percent from 10 percent in November despite Van Miert's warnings that it had better not try to take control of Lonrho's platinum interests based in South Africa.
The warnings came after the Commission blocked the planned merger of the platinum divisions of Lonrho and Gencor, the world's only other important player in the market.
Together, the three companies control 63 percent of the world's platinum output and 90 percent of the world's reserves. Platinum is used mainly in the manufacture of motor car catalytic converters.

Industry sources and competition experts believe that because Gencor itself has a significant stake in Lonrho's platinum division it will be even more difficult for the Commission to give the green light to Anglo.
"Instead of a duopoly, which the Commission already banned, you would have a virtual monopoly," a European antitrust official said.
But they also stressed that the Commission's preliminary assessment was based on the belief that Anglo has control of Lonrho -- something contested by the companies involved.
"A 27-percent ownership and one director does not give you control," an industry source said.
The Commission's conclusion arose from the study of previous public shareholders' meetings in companies with a similar ownership structure, the sources said.
One lawyer said Anglo had unsuccessfully tried to convince Lonrho to divest its platinum division altogether. But a Lonrho official denied there had been any pressure from Anglo to take such step.
Anglo requested Commission clearance for its 28-percent stake in Lonrho in November. In December, the Commission launched a full investigation into the case, which could last until May 5.
Other interested parties, such as the car sector or the jewellery industry -- another important user of platinum -- have still to be heard, probably later this month, the sources said.

The Commission has competence to vet all mergers and acquisitions that involve companies with a combined worldwide turnover of five billion European currency units and a European turnover of 250 million ecus each.
It has blocked seven deals since 1991 including the proposed Gencor/Lonrho platinum merger.
